en: This financing of the infrastructure combines with a logic of reward that, by contrast, has a marginal cost tending toward zero. If, in classical arrangements of political and social mobilization, loyalty can be bought with biological sustenance, here loyalty is captured through symbolic sustenance. Insignia, <1>skins</1>, emblems, passes, prestige levels and signs of distinction function as payment, but a payment that does not remunerate, it only regulates. The supplier exchanges lines of code and calibrated scarcity for hours of life, attention and behavioral predictability of the consumer, producing the cheapest form of bribery<2><3>240</3></2> yet observable in markets, since what is granted to the user has no intrinsic value independent of the ecosystem. On the contrary, its value depends on the very informational fief that issues it, which reinforces the circuit of permanence, since the reward received only “exists” as a recognizable difference within the controller's infrastructure.

Here, the Marxian rereading engages directly with the notion of semiotic vulnerability developed earlier. Exploitation operates not only at the economic level, but at the semiotic level. The platform controls the meanings attached to certain goods (a “legendary” <1>skin</1>, an “exclusive” title), defines which symbols confer status and belonging and determines what counts as legitimate progress within its ecosystem, which in turn encourages the user to invest so much lived experience in it that it can influence even how those meanings are understood outside its sphere of action and control. At the same time, it controls the mechanisms by which the consumer can lose these symbols, including <2>resets</2>, <3>meta</3> shifts, discontinued items and changes in the relative rarity of rewards. The fear of losing what has been accumulated, of seeing one's digital identity devalued or erased, becomes an instrument of discipline, consolidating a form of existential captivity that adds to the economic captivity already described.

<1>p. 225</1> This effect can be named, with operational precision, as identity captivity, understood as a modality of dependence in which the exit cost is not reduced to the patrimonial plane, but involves loss of recognition, of reputation and of narrative continuity objectified in public performance records, collections, histories and signs of distinction produced within the ecosystem. Dependence, in this register, is not psychological in the individualizing sense, but institutional and semiotic, because it stems from a regime of visibility and sanction that defines what counts as value, belonging and legitimate progress and, correlatively, defines how this can be downgraded, erased or disauthorized. In consumer-law terms, the relevance of the concept is not to create a new good, but to make controllable a specific form of loss in the fact of consumption, in which integrity of agency and symbolic identity are corroded by instability, opacity and manufactured risk, affecting the adequacy of the enjoyment regime and the legitimate trust that sustains continuous bonds governed by a platform.

In this key, the categories of digitally based businesses need to be treated as arrangements that organize the exploitation of this consumption “lumpenproletariat” and, at the same time, as structures that capture social coproduction and convert it into recurrent extraction through unilateral governance. A monetization model based on microtransactions for obtaining rare cosmetic items, for example, is not merely a commercial choice, but a device of value extraction that relies on the user's internalization of the logic of symbolic distinction produced by the platform and on the administration of the conditions of visibility and recognition that give economic meaning to rarity. The consumer pays to preserve or raise a position that exists only within the fief, in an economy whose currency is, at the same time, money and recognition, and in which the functional value equivalence of the Immaterial Object of Consumption is continually reconfigured to keep extraction ongoing.

Moreover, the incorporation of what is “outside” operates not only as economic fuel for the ecosystem, but also as an instrument for imposing order in practice. In regimes of platform governance, everyday discipline is not exercised only through written rules and formal sanctions, since it is sustained by the functional mobilization of collectives that simulate consensus, amplify official narratives, isolate dissent and, in certain circumstances, engage in reputational hostility and symbolic expulsion as a social extension of moderation decisions. The circuit closes when the infrastructure itself encourages and directs this mobilization (through visibility, ranking, recommendation, reporting and engagement mechanisms), turning the mass of users into an operational force capable of containing resistance, imposing exit costs and consolidating the regime of <1>p. 226</1> permanence<2><3>241</3></2>. It is in this sense that the “incorporated exterior” can operate as a political and policing tool in a structural sense, even without police, since coercion appears mediated by collective performance and the asymmetric protection of the apparatus<4><5>242</5></4>.

Besides capturing time and conduct as economic input, the platform mobilizes the incorporated exterior to perform a specific function in the reproduction of command, the capacity to improvise an audience. In structural terms, this is not merely spontaneous participation around a product, but a diffuse labor of staging adherence that manufactures visibility, normality and collective desire, turning a launch into an event and an event into social proof. <1>Hashtags</1>, engagement drives, event attendance, clips, reactions and micro-performances of enthusiasm operate as a symbolic infrastructure of valorization, since they turn an act of consumption into a public display of belonging and draw new users into the circuit of dependence. Productivity here is not only informational. It is scenographic, because it produces an artificial atmosphere of celebration that raises the perceived value of the offer and reduces reputational friction against the very architecture of extraction.

The political function of the incorporated exterior is not limited to the manufacture of a public and the production of social proof. It extends to community policing as an informal extension of governance. When criticisms of the model, of moderation decisions or of <1>p. 227</1> monetization practices emerge, the consumer himself, whose identity is in captivity<2><3>243</3></2> in the ecosystem, may act as a force of reputational intimidation and containment of dissent, not by explicit order, but by functional alignment between belonging and defense of the environment. Thus a device of diffuse private security is formed, in which fan “armies” operate to delegitimize critics, impose costs on speech, produce coordinated harassment and reinforce the official narrative, preserving the regime that exploits them in order to protect the symbolic coherence of their own position. Coercion, once again, appears without police, but with asymmetric protection of the apparatus, since the infrastructure of visibility, ranking and engagement amplifies informal policing and converts conflict into a mechanism of discipline.

The same logic deepens when one observes that the platform not only captures the user's behavior, but reabsorbs it as an internal function of the governance apparatus itself, that is, as a part of an organizational machinery that becomes autonomous and starts to operate as a practical condition of command<1><2>244</2></1>. The user comes to make up the machinery of valorization by producing social proof, by functioning as diffuse advertising, by maintaining routines of presence that stabilize metrics, by performing microtasks of curation and recommendation, by <3>p. 228</3> mass-testing changes of architecture (through behavioral “telemetry”) and, in certain segments, by supplying creative and communicational labor that is converted into an asset of the ecosystem. Thus, the boundary between public and operator becomes blurred, since the collective that should remain outside the center of command is, in practice, installed as a part of the governance circuit, and its participation comes to be exploited as a requirement for the functioning of the extraction regime. The cloud serf is not merely a captive consumer, because he is also an integrated component of the symbolic and economic administration of the fief, insofar as the apparatus feeds on his presence to regulate itself and to expand its own capacity for command.

The Marxian reading of the lumpenproletariat, in this framing, helps to set aside two inadequate simplifications. The first is to confuse exteriority with insignificance. The second is to treat the political usefulness of this layer as a merely episodic detail. Marx <1>(2011)</1> describes an unstable social mass that can be organized and activated as a practical device of power, operating in functions that cannot be reduced to regular productive labor, but that are decisive for the stabilization of a command and for the manufacture of public effects of legitimacy and order. It is this element (an instrumental functionalization of the “outside”) that directly interests the argument of the “incorporated exterior”<2><3>245</3></2>, because it allows exteriority to be treated not as an absence of link with valorization, but as a <4>p. 229</4> reconfigured link. The framing remains one of consumer law, since the homology operates as a tool for describing governance and mobilization in consumption, and not as a displacement of the object toward categories of labor.

It is precisely at this point that the structural parallelism with the platform economy gains density. The platform not only administers prices and catalog but also administers conduct, rhythms and presence. To do so, it needs to produce, continuously, public signs of adherence, normality and enthusiasm<1><2>246</2></1>, while neutralizing frictions and dissent that threaten retention and monetization. In functional terms, the user is integrated as part of this device, since, by engaging, reacting, ranking, recommending, reporting, moderating informally and reproducing patterns, he participates in the maintenance of the environment and its governability. The material incorporation of everyday life as input is not limited to data as information, since it includes behavior as an organizing force of the platform's social space, that is, as an operative component of government.

In this register, the analogy operates as a key to intelligibility. Marx <1>(2011)</1> describes the organization of the lumpenproletariat as a force capable of improvising a public, simulating enthusiasm, intimidating opponents and acting with institutional tolerance/protection, functioning as a gear for the performance of power and the manufacture of consensus in act<2><3>247</3></2>. The <4>p. 230</4> usefulness of the passage lies not in importing nineteenth-century categories as if they were the sociological identity of the contemporary user, but in recognizing the recurrent structure: layers socially “external” to regular productive labor can be mobilized as instruments of government and as a technology for stabilizing command, including when their activity appears under the guise of spontaneity, leisure, sociability or “community participation”.

Transposed to the environment of IOCs, this structure helps to explain why rentier extraction requires more than charging: it requires an architecture of permanence. The platform calibrates what counts as visibility, what counts as reputation, what belonging is and what represents normality in the ecosystem, and it does so by converting the very circulation of users into a mechanism of ordering. Thus, the cloud serf is kept simultaneously as a recurrent payer and as a diffuse producer of stability for the fief, since he sustains the valuation of the environment through engagement and sustains the governance of the environment through the everyday production of signs, <1>rankings</1> and informal discipline. The legal-structural consequence is direct, because, when the platform comes to depend on the continuous mobilization of the user to govern and to valorize the ecosystem, it gains systemic incentives to design scarcity, risk and sanction so as to produce presence, and not merely purchase.

The Marxian tradition describes capitalism as a social form capable of incorporating collective and organizational conditions into the logic of valorization<1><2>248</2></1>, converting direction, <3>p. 231</3> coordination and reproduction into internal functions of the process<4><5>249</5></4>. Applied to the environment of IOCs, this means that extraction is not limited to price. It depends on keeping enjoyment under governance and on transforming the presence of users into a condition of stability of the ecosystem<6><7>250</7></6>. The consequence is that the economic purpose of the model materializes as <8>p. 232</8> institutional design, that is, as architectural teleology oriented toward retention and continuous capture.

Missions are communally described as “Do something, get something” systems, with the explanation that the player completes specific objectives and receives rewards, with progress being tracked. The definition is useful because it shows the didactic way in which the platform naturalizes the transformation of conduct into a criterion of access to internal value <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2017d)</2>. <3>↩</3>

The contract provides that the license to access Game Currency or Virtual Content may be acquired by purchase, by earning or by receipt, and makes “earning” explicit as the completion of “missions or game tasks”. The note is probative because it records that the circuit of tasks does not present itself as mere ornamental <1>design</1>, but as a formal category of access to internal value <2>Riot Games</2><3>(Riot Games, 2024e)</3>. <4>↩</4>

On missions as a deliberate technology of conduction and adjustment. In the text <1>/dev: Missions Update</1>, a mission system as something that was launched and has been adjusted based on mission types, difficulties and objectives, discussing “takeaways” and “struggles” of the design, qualifying missions as a technology of conduction that evolves into the function of an engagement tool, and not a mere aesthetic or narrative adornment <2>Riot Games</2><3>(Riot Games, 2017f)</3>. <4>↩</4>

On the <1>PBE</1> as a stage of public testing and capture of diffuse labor. In official support, the <2>PBE</2> is described as a server on which one can “test upcoming features” and that allows the company to “eliminate any bugs” found “before it is implemented in the game environment” <3>Riot Games</3><4>(Riot Games, 2024j)</4>. <5>↩</5>

On the contractual appropriation of informational contributions without consideration. In Clause 6.1, the contract states that “We value your feedback”, but prohibits its submission and, if submitted, provides that the company may “freely use” the ideas and do so “without any payment to you” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>. <3>↩</3>

In announcing the closed beta phase of new partnership programs, Riot presents the initiative as a way to “offer more support to creators” and to grant “exclusive benefits”, structuring a selective regime of access and advantage oriented toward the community production of content, without this becoming a wage relationship, a duty of continuity or stability for those who, in practice, sustain part of the intelligibility of the ecosystem <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2025m)</2>. <3>↩</3>

“<1>Client</1>” designates the <2>software</2> component through which the user accesses the service, its interfaces and operational routines (authentication, updating, purchase, inventory, social etc.). The term <3>client</3> is chosen to avoid confusion with “cliente” in Portuguese, which refers primarily to the economic subject of the consumer relationship. Here, the focus is not the subject, but the technical-mediating artifact — the application that operationalizes the experience and materializes choices, notifications and restrictions. <4>↩</4>

On a social network, a publicly identified developer frames the tests of <1>skin previews</1> with the question “Tired of not knowing what you’re buying?”, acknowledging that the lack of preview instruments is a real problem of the offer architecture. The relevant point here is not the announcement itself, but the admission that, for long periods, purchasing operated with low auditability within the very flow of the <2>client</2>, pushing verification outside the developer's circuit <3>RIOTMIKOUZ</3><4>(RiotMikouz, 2025)</4>. <5>↩</5>

The SkinSpotlights channel has established itself as a recurring “showcase” window for skins on the YouTube platform, displaying visual effects, animations, recalls and variations, functioning as a practical source of visualization for consumers who seek to understand the experience of the item before buying. When this mediation becomes a normal condition of decision, it ceases to be mere “community content” and comes to operate as informational infrastructure necessary for consumption <1>SKINSPOTLIGHTS</1><2>(SkinSpotlights, 2026)</2>. <3>↩</3>

The contract defines that the license granted to the user is for “personal, non-commercial” use and conditioned on compliance with the instrument itself, which frames content production as a practice dependent on authorization, exceptions and institutional programs, instead of recognition as an ordinary economic activity of the ecosystem <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>. <3>↩</3>

The expression “incorporated exterior” is used here to designate a form of functional integration of agents socially external to the regular circuit of productive labor and institutional legitimacy: it is someone “from outside” who is not merely tolerated, but converted into an internal gear of the regime, including through the occupation and capture of positions within the public machine. Marx describes this mechanism by showing how Bonapartism is not limited to mobilizing the bohème as an episodic support troop, but injects it into the institutions, transforming it into a political and administrative body of power, with material effects on the practices of the State and on the very economy of command. “Bonaparte would like to be seen as the patriarchal benefactor of all classes. But he cannot give to one without taking from another. [...] He would like to steal all of France in order to give it as a present to France or, rather, in order to be able to buy France back with French money, because, as chief of the Society of December 10, he must be able to pay for what he intends to possess. And the institution of purchase comes to be integrated by all the institutions of the State: the Senate, the Council of State, the Legislature, the Legion of Honor, the military medals, the public baths, the public buildings, the railways, the état-major [General Staff] of the National Guard without a commune, the confiscated estates of the house of Orléans. [...] The court, the ministries, the head posts of the administration and of the army are besieged and seized by a band of individuals, of the best of whom it can be said that no one knows where he comes from; it is a noisy, disreputable and predatory bohème that crawls in gala garments with the same elegant posture as the high dignitaries of Soulouque.’” <1>Marx</1><2>(Marx, 2011, [p. 94])</2> <3>↩</3>
In the works O 18 de Brumário de Luís Bonaparte (2011) and O Capital (2013). <1>↩</1>

Marx describes the lumpenproletariat, in the context of the Bonapartist organization, as a heterogeneous and unstable social ensemble, formed by displaced and marginal strata, whose unity does not derive from regular insertion in productive labor, but from its availability for instrumental organization under command. The long list of social types does not have a merely descriptive function, since it evidences the absence of stable structure and the condition of a mobilizable mass, whose political functionality becomes possible precisely because of its disaggregation and its lateral position in relation to the ordinary forms of production and representation. It is this social form, marked by indefiniteness, destructuring and directed mobilization, that matters here as a structural homology for thinking about contemporary modalities of incorporating subjects formally external to regular productive labor into regimes of extraction and power. In the author's words: “This society dates from the year 1849. Under the pretext of founding a benevolent society, the Parisian lumpenproletariat was organized into secret sections, each of them led by a Bonapartist agent and with a Bonapartist general at the top. Decayed roués [ruffians] with doubtful means of subsistence and of doubtful origin, ruined and adventurous offshoots of the bourgeoisie were flanked by vagabonds, discharged soldiers, ex-convicts, slaves escaped from the galleys, swindlers, tricksters, lazzaroni [lazzaroni], pickpockets, conjurers, gamblers, maquereaux [pimps], brothel keepers, porters, literati, organ grinders, ragpickers, knife grinders, tinkers, beggars, in short, that whole indefinite, destructured mass thrown hither and thither, which the French call la bohème [the bohème]; with these elements, akin to him, Bonaparte formed the basis of the Society of December 10. It was a ‘benevolent society’ insofar as all its members, like Bonaparte, felt the need to benefit themselves at the expense of the laboring nation.” <1>Marx</1><2>(Marx, 2011, [p. 57])</2>. <3>↩</3>

Here, the word “bribery” is used metaphorically to describe how consumer loyalty is captured through a "symbolic sustenance", in which the supplier exchanges mere lines of code and calibrated scarcity for hours of the user's life and attention. The practice is qualified as the cheapest form of coercion ever observed in markets, since the rewards offered, such as insignia and cosmetic items, have no intrinsic value outside the ecosystem and depend entirely on the controller's infrastructure to exist, reinforcing a circuit of permanence that converts the individual's participation into an input of valorization for the platform. <1>↩</1>

It is recorded, as a hypothesis of extension to be tested in later works, that the notion of “incorporated exterior” does not depend on the specific domain analyzed here, but describes a recurrent structural position in intermediation platforms and in private governance by architecture. In arrangements of this nature, the operation of the service presupposes the participation of subjects formally external to the organization, whose activity makes up the available offer, the experience delivered and, often, the very mechanisms of trust and legitimacy of the environment (for example, through reputation, ratings, performance metrics and signs of credibility). Although they remain external on the legal-organizational plane, such agents are incorporated on the economic and operational plane as indispensable infrastructure, under conditions of informational and power asymmetry. From this perspective, incorporation is not limited to the use of data or the capture of attention: it is expressed in the platform's capacity to modulate access, visibility, priority, remuneration, reach and permanence by means of mutable rules, ranking criteria, compliance automatisms and technically executed sanctions. The result is a regime in which relevant costs, risks and contingencies tend to be shifted to the incorporated exterior (including risks of demand variation, reputational exposure, evidentiary contestation, unilateral changes and functional interruptions), while the platform reserves for itself the power of coordination, the informational advantage and the prerogative of defining the conditions of participation and value extraction. <1>↩</1>

The idea of “incorporation” that underpins the notion of “incorporated exterior” is not reduced to diffuse adherence or symbolic support. In Marx, it appears as material incorporation by organizational means: socially unstable layers external to regular productive labor are mobilized as an auxiliary force (military and police) to produce decisive effects on the correlation of forces, including the physical repression of the proletariat. It is in this sense — of the practical functionalization of the “outside” as an instrument for stabilizing order — that the lumpenproletariat can be described as a gear incorporated into certain arrangements of power. “The bourgeois republic triumphed. It had the support of the financial aristocracy, the industrial bourgeoisie, the middle class, the petty bourgeois, the army, the lumpenproletariat organized as the mobile guard, the intellectual capacities, the priestlings and the rural population. On the side of the Parisian proletariat there was no one but itself. […] More than 3 thousand insurgents were butchered after the victory, 15 thousand were deported without trial.” <1>Marx</1><2>(Marx, 2011, [p. 26])</2> <3>↩</3>
The discussion of identity captivity is deepened in section 4.2.3 Psychopolitics, self-exploitation and identity captivity. <1>↩</1>

The notion of “apparatus” is mobilized here in a structural sense. Not as a vague metaphor, but as a form of bureaucratic-administrative organization that becomes autonomous from society and can be appropriated as political spoils. “This Executive Power with its monstrous bureaucratic and military organization, with its multifaceted and artful state machine, this army of officials of half a million people added to a regular army of another half million, this terrible corporation of parasites, which envelops the organism of French society like a membrane and clogs all its pores, arose in the time of absolute monarchy, in the epoch of the decline of the feudal system, whose acceleration it helped bring about. The seigneurial privileges of the landowners and the towns are transformed into as many attributes of state power, the feudal dignitaries become paid officials and the motley catalog of conflicting medieval potentates is converted into the regulated plan of a state power whose work is divided and centralized as in a factory. The first French revolution, in fulfilling the task of breaking all autonomous powers at the local, territorial, urban and provincial levels, aiming to create bourgeois national unity, necessarily developed what absolute monarchy had begun: centralization and, along with it, the radius of action, the attributes and the servants of governmental power. Napoleon perfected this machine of the State. This legitimate monarchy and the July Monarchy added nothing but a greater division of labor, which grew in the same proportion as the division of labor within bourgeois society created new interest groups, that is, new material for state administration. Every common interest was immediately detached from society and set against it as a higher, general interest, withdrawn from the activity of society's own members and transformed into an object of governmental activity, from the bridge, the schoolhouse and the communal property of a village to the railways, the national property and the national university of France. The parliamentary republic, finally, in its struggle against the revolution, found itself obliged to reinforce the means and the centralization of governmental power in order to implement repressive measures. All revolutions only perfected the machine instead of breaking it. The parties that fought alternately for power regarded the seizure of this monstrous state edifice as the lion's share of the victor's spoils.” <1>Marx</1><2>(Marx, 2011, p. 87)</2>. In The Eighteenth Brumaire, Marx describes the modern Executive Power as a historically accumulated bureaucratic-military state machine, endowed with its own dynamics, and whose control appears, repeatedly, as the “lion's share” of the victor's spoils — a point that supports, by functional homology, the reading that governance regimes can reabsorb external agents as internal functions of the apparatus of command. <3>↩</3>

In deepening the relationship between Bonaparte and the lumpenproletariat, Marx not only describes the social composition of this layer, but makes explicit its singular political usefulness. It is the only support that can be mobilized “unconditionally” by a power that is not anchored in a stable way in the institutional legitimacy of the propertied classes or in the regular forms of representation. The argument is relevant because it allows two things to be separated: the condition of socioeconomic marginality and social heterogeneity; and its functionalization as a privileged political support for a form of command that feeds precisely on instability, opportunism and the availability to adhere to a logic of immediate benefit. Thus, the “affinity” between leader and base is neither psychological nor moral; it is structural, in the sense that the regime finds in this layer a support less conditioned by class commitments, by regular forms of labor and by expectations of institutional order, operating as a vector of direct sustenance of command. According to Marx <1>(2011, [p. 57-58])</1>: “This Bonaparte constitutes himself as chief of the lumpenproletariat, because it is in it that he identifies en masse the interests he pursues personally, recognizing, in this scum, this waste, this refuse of all classes, the only class on which he can rely unconditionally; this is the real Bonaparte, the Bonaparte sans phrase [without retouching]. As an old and crafty roué, he conceives the historical existence of peoples and their great official actions as comedy in the most ordinary sense possible, as a masquerade in which the fine costumes, the words and the grandiloquent gestures serve only to conceal the most petty knavery. This is what happened in the expedition to Strasbourg, in which a trained Swiss vulture played the part of the Napoleonic eagle. In his attack on Boulogne, he dressed some London lackeys in French uniform, who played the part of the Armed Forces. In his Society of December 10, he gathered 10 thousand lumpens who were to represent the people in the same way that Klaus Zettel represented the lion. At the moment when the bourgeoisie itself came to stage the most complete comedy, albeit with unsurpassable seriousness, without violating any of the pedantic conditions of French dramatic etiquette, itself half deceived and half convinced of the solemn character of its great official actions, the adventurer who regarded this action as pure comedy was bound to triumph. Only after having eliminated his solemn adversary, only after he himself began to take his imperial role seriously and, putting on the Napoleonic mask, imagined he was representing the real Napoleon, did he become the victim of his own worldview, the serious clown, who ceases to take universal history as comedy and comes to see his comedy as universal history.” <2>↩</2>

The question does not involve describing a contingent psychological manipulation, but making explicit a mechanism of social form. Relations between people (collective adherence, reputation, comparison, recognition, belonging) are reconfigured and returned to the participants themselves under the appearance of objective properties of the ecosystem (metrics, rankings, prestige, “trends”, “relevance”), as if they were natural attributes of the environment and not results of a mediated social organization. This inversion is compatible with the Marxian description of fetishism, in which a determinate social relation assumes, for the subjects, the form of a relation between things, obscuring its constructed character and naturalizing the regime as if it were an objective given of the world. “The mysterious character of the commodity-form consists, therefore, simply in the fact that it reflects to men the social characters of their own labor as objective characters of the products of labor themselves, as social properties that are natural to these things and, therefore, it also reflects the social relation of the producers to total labor as a social relation between objects, existing apart from the producers. It is through this quid pro quo that the products of labor become commodities, sensible-suprasensible or social things. The luminous impression of a thing on the optic nerve does not present itself, then, as a subjective stimulus of the optic nerve itself, but as the objective form of a thing that is outside the eye. In the act of seeing, however, the light of a thing, of an external object, is effectively cast upon another thing, the eye. It is a physical relation between physical things. The commodity-form and the value relation of the products of labor in which it is represented have, on the contrary, absolutely nothing to do with their physical nature and with the material [dinglichen] relations that result from it. It is only a determinate social relation between men themselves that here assumes, for them, the phantasmagoric form of a relation between things. Thus, to find an analogy, we must take refuge in the nebulous region of the religious world. Here, the products of the human brain appear endowed with a life of their own, as autonomous figures that maintain relations with one another and with men. So it is, in the world of commodities, with the products of the human hand. This I call fetishism, which attaches itself to the products of labor as soon as they are produced as commodities and which is, therefore, inseparable from the production of commodities.” <1>Marx</1><2>(Marx, 2013, p. 206-207)</2>. <3>↩</3>

“What the National Workshops represented for the socialist workers, what the Gardes mobiles represented for the republican bourgeois, the Society of December 10 was for Bonaparte, his typical partisan armed force. On his journeys, detachments of this force, in crammed railway carriages, had to improvise a public for him, display public enthusiasm, bellow vive l'Empereur [long live the emperor], insult and beat the republicans, obviously counting on the protection of the police. On his return journeys to Paris, it was to form the vanguard, forestall counter-demonstrations or disperse them. The Society of December 10 belonged to him, it was his work, his exclusive idea. Everything else he appropriates is handed to him by the force of circumstances, everything else he does is done for him by the correlation of facts or he contents himself with copying the deeds of others; but his official speeches on order, religion, family and property, delivered publicly before the citizens, backed by the secret society of the Schufterles and Spiegelbergs, the society of disorder, prostitution and thievery: this is Bonaparte himself as original author, and the history of the Society of December 10 is his own history.” <1>Marx</1><2>(Marx, 2011, [p. 58])</2>. Marx describes, in the Bonapartist case, a mechanism of political incorporation of a heterogeneous social mass that acts as a practical instrument of power: not only as a symbolic base of support, but as an operational force intended to produce public effects (applause, “enthusiasm”, intimidation) and to neutralize opponents, with institutional protection and tolerance. The passage is evidence that the functionalization of the lumpenproletariat is not limited to “making up the scenery”, since it integrates the regime as a technology of government. It is a category that functions as an arm of intervention, proving capable of organizing presence, disciplining social space and manufacturing signs of legitimacy. This supports a structural reading of the phenomenon, given that the marginal layer is instrumentalized as a device of action external to the regular forms and that is, even so, decisive for conferring stability on the command held by the platform. <3>↩</3>

The description of capitalism as a social form in which the dynamics of value organizes the process is not reduced to the trivial idea of “pursuit of profit”. The core is that, in specifically capitalist circulation, commodity and money function as modes of existence of value itself and the movement comes to operate as self-valorization, that is, as a process that imposes itself as the “subject” of the circuit. This formulation is useful here because it allows coordination, governance and the administration of conditions of enjoyment to be treated as functions subordinated to the dynamics of valorization, and not as simple contingent management choices. “The independent forms, the money-forms that the value of commodities assumes in simple circulation serve only as mediation for the exchange of commodities and disappear in the result of the movement. In the circulation M-C-M, on the contrary, commodity and money function only as different modes of existence of value itself: money as its universal mode of existence, the commodity as its particular, so to speak, disguised mode of existence. Value passes constantly from one form to another, without being lost in this movement, and thereby becomes the automatic subject of the process. Now, if we take the particular forms of manifestation that self-valorizing value successively assumes in the course of its life, we arrive at these two propositions: capital is money and capital is commodity. In truth, however, value here becomes the subject of a process in which, beneath its constant variation of form, appearing now as money, now as commodity, it alters its own magnitude and, as surplus value, repels [abstösst] itself as original value and valorizes itself. For the movement in which it adds surplus value is its own movement; its valorization is, therefore, self-valorization. Because it is value, it has received the occult quality of adding value. It gives birth to offspring, or at least lays golden eggs.” <1>Marx</1><2>(Marx, 2013, p. 297)</2>. <3>↩</3>

The incorporation of collective conditions into the process of valorization does not occur only through the “aggregate” economic result of joint labor, but through the transformation of the very need for direction and supervision into an internal function of capital. When labor assumes cooperative form on a large scale, coordination ceases to be a simple neutral technical requirement and comes to express, under capitalism, a specific function: ordering social labor according to the purpose of self-valorization and according to the antagonism between exploiter and exploited material. It is in this sense that “direction” and “command” do not appear as an element external to the process, but as a constitutive dimension of the capitalist mode of production. “All immediately social or collective labor on a large scale requires, to a greater or lesser extent, a direction that establishes harmony among individual activities and performs the general functions that result from the movement of the total productive body as distinct from the movement of its autonomous organs. A single violinist directs himself, but an orchestra requires a conductor. This function of direction, supervision and mediation becomes a function of capital as soon as the labor subordinated to it becomes cooperative. As a specific function of capital, direction assumes specific characteristics. First, the motive that drives and the purpose that determines the capitalist production process is the greatest possible self-valorization of capital, that is, the greatest possible production of surplus value and, therefore, the maximum possible exploitation of labor power by the capitalist. As the mass of simultaneously employed workers increases, so does their resistance and, with it, the pressure of capital to overcome it. The command of the capitalist is not only a specific function, arising from the nature of the social labor process and, therefore, peculiar to that process, but, at the same time, a function of exploitation of a social labor process, and is, for that reason, determined by the inevitable antagonism between the exploiter and the raw material of his exploitation.” <1>Marx</1><2>(Marx, 2013, p. 504)</2>. <3>↩</3>

The idea of “incorporated exterior” gains precision when one considers that, in the Marxian tradition, activities that seem situated outside the immediate core of production, such as individual consumption and the very everyday reproduction of labor power, can be treated as internal moments of the reproduction of capital. This is not a metaphor, since the consumption that keeps the worker fit to work is described as a functional element of the process, even though it takes place outside the factory. With this, Marx provides a formal scheme especially useful for this research, since capitalism does not depend only on what happens “within” the productive act, but on capturing and organizing external social conditions as requirements for the continuity of valorization. On the plane of IOCs, the structural analogy is not to assert that the user “is an industrial worker”, but rather to recognize that the platform converts presence, routine and consumption into conditions for the reproduction of its own economic circuit. “The worker's consumption has a double nature. In production itself, he consumes, by means of his labor, means of production, transforming them into products of greater value than that of the capital advanced. This is his productive consumption. At the same time, it is consumption of his labor power by the capitalist who bought it. On the other hand, the worker spends on means of subsistence the money paid for the purchase of labor power: this is his individual consumption. […] The worker is often forced to convert his individual consumption into a mere incident of the production process. In that case, he supplies himself with means of subsistence to keep his labor power running, in the same way as the steam engine is supplied with coal and water and the wheel with oil. […] When the capitalist converts part of his capital into labor power, he thereby valorizes his total capital and kills two birds with one stone. He profits not only from what he receives from the worker, but also from what he gives him. The capital alienated in exchange for labor power is converted into means of subsistence, whose consumption serves to reproduce the muscles, nerves, bones and brain of existing workers and to produce new workers. […] Such consumption is production and reproduction of the means of production most indispensable to the capitalist: the worker himself. The individual consumption of the worker thus remains a moment of the production and reproduction of capital, whether it is carried out inside or outside the workshop, the factory etc.” <1>Marx</1><2>(Marx, 2013, p. 787-788)</2>. <3>↩</3>

<1>Social function of intellectual property</1>

The engineering of scarcity and risk described does not operate in a vacuum, since it reorganizes the very grammar of competition. When the economic object ceases to be a material good, delivered and circulable as a thing, and becomes a continuous immaterial good, mediated by platform, account, catalog, interface and access rules, what is contested among economic agents changes in nature. Instead of competing only on productive efficiency, on price or on the intrinsic quality of a product, what comes to matter is controlling access, that is, defining who enters, where they enter, under what conditions they remain and at what cost they manage to leave.

The competitive mutation described manifests itself clearly in interactive entertainment operated by platform because competitive value is not concentrated in the “quality” of an isolated good, but in the capacity to keep the consumer bound to a proprietary grammar of belonging, progress and distinction. In the ecosystem of an <1>online</1> game, cosmetic items and <2>reworks</2> do not function as peripheral “accessories”, but as pieces of an economy of identity that depends on social visibility, comparison and recognition within the environment itself. Economic rivalry, in this framework, shifts to the administration of the gateways to these layers of meaning, to the distribution circuits (rotating shops, events, passes, availability windows) and to the raising of migration costs, since the investment is not transferable outside the technical fief. What is contested, therefore, is the infrastructure that makes the promise consumable, and not merely the promise in the abstract.

For this reason, competition in platform economies tends to assume an asymmetric design, shifting from the contest over products to the contest over a position of <1>gatekeeping</1> over technical and symbolic ecosystems. When economic power is concentrated in the capacity to intermediate flows of attention, data, reputation, digital libraries and routines of use, competition ceases to function as a simple alternation of consumer preferences and comes to function as competition for entrapment by <2>design</2>. “Market power” exceeds the field of share in sales, becoming command over the very infrastructure in which the consumer's “choice” becomes possible.

<1>p. 233</1> Competition in markets for material goods tends to preserve structural frictions that limit the consolidation of a fully stable dominance, even if they do not prevent it entirely. Installed capacity, logistics, marginal costs, access to inputs and productive dispersion function, as a rule, as brakes that make leadership relevant, but more contestable over time. Even where there are concentration and durable advantages, the contest remains anchored in physical and organizational constraints that impose real costs of expansion and of maintaining command.

In platform-mediated immaterial goods and services, the dynamics reorganize because part of these frictions is replaced by concentration mechanisms peculiar to digital infrastructure. Non-rivalry and reproducibility at reduced marginal cost do not eliminate competition, but shift the terrain of the contest toward network effects, <1>lock-in</1>, standardization of interfaces and protocols, economies of informational scale and accumulation of data. The dominant position thus tends to stabilize less through efficiency in an isolated product and more through control of the channel, of access and of the conditions of enjoyment, which reconfigures the very competitive grammar.

Technology giants, such as <1>Amazon</1> in certain <2>online</2> retail markets and cloud services, or <3>Mercado Livre</3> in the intermediation of electronic commerce in specific regions, not only lead, but in many cases define and control the very infrastructure on which competition (or its appearance) takes place. This dominance does not rest only on the productive efficiency of a specific good, but on the strategic control of networks, data, algorithms and, above all, of attention and of access to the consumer, elements that characterize the informational domination and digital rentierism previously discussed. The capacity of a single entity to control the entirety of an immaterial good or its main access route reconfigures the economic order with profound sociopolitical implications.

If immaterial competition tends to produce structural winners, it becomes necessary to explain why this victory proves not merely contingent, but stabilizable. In material goods, domination faces physical and social frictions (installed capacity, logistics, sources of input, productive dispersion). In digital ecosystems, however, the very access route to the good coincides with the private infrastructure that organizes it. In this scenario, economic power is consolidated not only through efficiency, but through governance, since controlling the gate amounts to controlling the market, insofar as the gate becomes the market itself.

The scenario ceases to be merely an example and reveals itself as a typical case of competition by enclosure. The “rare” cosmetic item is not rare by technical nature, since its reproduction is <1>p. 234</1> trivial, but because the platform administers scarcity, prestige and circulation as internal variables of the market itself, converting technical abundance into economic scarcity. The unilateral alteration of the item's appearance, effects or place in the internal economy, as in the scenario described, operates as an exercise of competitive power because it redefines <2>ex post </2>the meaning and utility of the good within the proprietary language, without the consumer having an equivalent route of restoration outside the ecosystem. Competition thus comes to function as a contest for sovereignty over signs and for the capacity to rewrite, over time, what “is worth” and what “delivers”, shifting consumer protection to a terrain in which control of the market is inseparable from control of the semantics of consumption itself.

In practical terms, this persistence arises from the combination of network effects, <1>lock-</1><2>in</2>, standardization of interfaces and protocols, economies of informational scale and accumulation of data, which convert preference into dependence and make spontaneous competitive contestation structurally improbable.

It is here that intellectual property rights cease to appear as a peripheral legal title and come to operate as a material component of the architecture of closure. The decisive economic point is simple and direct, since, in the market for immaterial goods, reproducibility would tend to dissolve price, so that rent depends on reintroducing scarcity by institutional decision. When this decision is coupled with license contracts, accounts, <1>DRM</1><2><3>251</3></2>, catalogs and authentication mechanisms, the incentive to create gives way to a technology of blocking, so that circulation comes to be treated as infringement and enjoyment is converted into authorization. In this context, competition ceases to be only a contest over products and becomes a contest over enclosures.

If competition, in the immaterial, tends to produce structural winners through capture of the channel, what remains to be explained is the legal mechanism that stabilizes this victory over time. It is here that intellectual property, coupled with infrastructure and contracts, ceases to be only a title and comes to function as a competitive technology of enclosure.

The stabilization of competitive victory in immaterial markets requires converting technical abundance into socially constructed scarcity, because the reproducibility of the immaterial would tend to dissolve price and, with it, the possibility of rent, if there is no institutional decision to reinstall barriers. Intellectual property ceases to operate only as an incentive and becomes part of an arrangement of enclosure, functioning as a true <1>p. 235</1> “legal latifundium”<2><3>252</3></2> that immobilizes accumulated technologies and knowledge under titles of prolonged exclusivity <4>Dowbor</4><5>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 44)</5>. When this latifundium is coupled with license contracts, accounts, DRM, catalogs and authentication mechanisms, the incentive to create gives way to a technology of blocking and the objective of copyright comes to operate as a mechanism for closing access<6><7>253</7></6>, transforming access into a conditional license and enjoyment into a precarious authorization, continually reconfigurable, insofar as circulation comes to be treated as infringement <8>Dowbor</8><9>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 44)</9>.

The consequence, for consumption, is that what gives concreteness to the consumer's right is not the possession of <1>bits</1>, but the legal materiality of the object<2><3>254</3></2>, understood as stability and predictability of the practical conditions that make enjoyment possible over time, in an environment in which economic control shifts from the good to the process and utility depends on continuous governance under private dominion <4>Dowbor</4><5>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51-52)</5>. It is an institutional concreteness, since the infrastructure and the mechanisms that sustain access, circulation and continuity remain under the control of platforms and their governance systems <6>Dowbor</6><7>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 8; p. 51-52)</7>. The decisive economic point is that, in the immaterial, reproducibility would tend to dissolve price, and this inversion is particularly sensitive in the networked environment, because copying is not a deviation, but an ordinary technical condition of <8>p. 236</8> enjoyment itself, insofar as copying is part of transmission, storage, caching and, in a certain sense, reading itself <9>Dowbor</9><10>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51)</10>. By legally requalifying this constitutive gesture, intellectual property ceases to operate only as an incentive and comes to function as a technology of blocking, since it transforms circulation into infringement and enjoyment into authorization, allowing the supplier to govern the experience of the IOC as precarious and modulable access <11>Dowbor</11><12>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51)</12>.

This logic of enclosure and informational toll finds critical and paradigmatic application in the examination of contractual clauses that grant developers the automatic appropriation of derivative works and user-generated content. The phenomenon is not an isolated topic of intellectual property, since it constitutes a concrete manifestation of artificial scarcity applied to cultural platforms, as the supplier uses its infrastructure to capture the symbolic surplus<1><2>255</2></1>, that is, the value generated in the very use and circulation of signs in the ecosystem, such as reputation, belonging, styles, narratives and visibility. The economic centrality of this surplus is described by Dowbor, following Gorz, in the analysis of the brand, of advertising and of symbolic values as the basis of a new formation of value <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 23)</4>. Produced by users under the rule of standard clauses, this cultural and collaborative flow is recast as a private infrastructure of rent, which reinforces the supplier's command over circulation and enjoyment in the ecosystem.

When the platform already occupies a <1>gatekeeper</1> position, intellectual property and license contracts cease to be a legal detail and come to operate as a device of economic government of the ecosystem. The competitive effect is direct, because it is not enough to offer a better product when the dominant operator defines what counts as legitimate use, which practices are tolerated, who may circulate signs and on what terms. Thus, intellectual <2>p. 237</2> property does not act only as exclusivity over an asset, since it functions as a rule of entry and permanence in an environment in which enjoyment itself depends on continuous authorization. What is consolidated is an economy of cumulative permissions, in which each portion of access functions as a key, and the accumulation of keys is converted into market power.

Enclosure becomes particularly visible when one observes the point at which consumption is converted into production within the ecosystem. On cultural platforms and, paradigmatically, in game ecosystems, value lies not only in what is sold to the consumer, but also in what the consumer circulates, such as derivative works, content, styles, tutorials, mods, narratives, reputation and prestige. When standard clauses transform this flow into automatic appropriation by the platform, competition ceases to be only a contest over supply and becomes a contest over the capture of the cultural surplus produced within the market itself.

This logic of enclosure and informational toll finds paradigmatic application in the examination of contractual clauses that grant developers the automatic appropriation of derivative works and user-generated content (UGC). Although UGC models may require licenses functionally necessary for the circulation of content in the ecosystem, the legal problem emerges when the standard authorization expands beyond what is necessary and is converted into automatic appropriation of the content generated by the user, transferring to the platform the ownership of creative interactions and derivative works produced in the course of use.

At this point, the supplier not only charges for access, but captures symbolic surplus and creative labor from the consumer, reinforcing the toll economy over the cultural base of the ecosystem, without proportional reciprocity and under the unilateral governance of the rightholder<1><2>256</2></1>. It is not, therefore, a simple reservation of rights, but an architecture that recasts collaborative effort and social participation as a private infrastructure for generating rent.

From the competitive point of view, what is at stake here is not only “who has the best content”, but who controls the conditions under which content can exist, circulate and be reused. When the platform captures UGC and derivative works by default, it is not <1>p. 238</1> only appropriating cultural value produced within the ecosystem: it is expanding its <2>gatekeeping</2> power over the very horizon of creation and circulation of signs in that market. Intellectual Property, then, does not operate only as one-off exclusivity, but as an infrastructure for stabilizing victory in the competitive “tournament”. It fixes the advantage over time by transforming access and reuse into a regime of continuous authorization. The duration and elasticity of these rights cease to be a technical detail and become part of the economic core of enclosure. Extending terms and expanding scopes means prolonging the toll and reducing the space for contestation through spontaneous competitive mechanisms.

Dowbor associates the problem of Intellectual Property not only with the existence of the right itself, but with its historical extension under organized pressure, observing that “we will only have digital access to a work 70 years after the author's death” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 43)</2> and questioning whether very long copyrights and “indefinitely extended” rights are disseminating culture or, on the contrary, hindering the social process <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 46)</4>. The argument is one of political economy, since, if the realization of profit is concentrated mostly in the first years of commercial exploitation <5>Dowbor</5><6>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 43)</6>, maintaining exclusivity for decades operates as rent without a proportional incentivizing function<7><8>257</8></7> and imposes a massive social cost on research and creative reuse to sustain concentrated private flows. In this context, time becomes a deliberate mechanism of rentierism, because extending protection terms means, in practice, prolonging the toll on the common heritage of humanity.

A critical point of Dowbor's argumentative axis lies in the distinction between the figure of the creator and that of the rentier. The author, as subject of intellectual creation, has little to do with this dynamic, since the rights almost always belong to intermediaries <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 44)</2>. The finding shifts the focus of the discussion. It is not, strictly speaking, a matter of ensuring the artist's remuneration, but of identifying a chain of intermediation that converts copyright into a financializable asset and administers access to the good in a structurally captive market. From this perspective, intellectual property reveals itself as a legal platform of extraction, <3>p. 239</3> because whoever holds the title holds, at the same time, the turnstile of access. In this arrangement, the moral discourse of theft comes to function as a tool of legitimation. Through guilt and criminalization, it sustains charging for the circulation of goods whose use by one individual does not reduce availability to another.

Dowbor makes explicit that the proliferation and overlapping of IP rights can produce prohibitive transaction costs and block subsequent innovations by “placing multiple obstacles” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 47)</2>, configuring a tragedy of the anticommons<3><4>258</4></3>. The fragmentation of exclusivities distributes veto powers and makes recombination legally improbable or economically unviable, even if the resource remains technically available. This is not only an ethical critique, but a technical-institutional diagnosis. When an innovation depends on the articulation of multiple protected components, the creative process comes to require fragmented legal negotiation, with licenses, rights regularization (<5>clearance</5>) and constant risks of litigation. Structural friction favors large actors endowed with robust legal capacity and excludes smaller innovators, resulting in an ecosystem in which creativity remains subordinated to proprietary governance and to control over what has already been created.

The thesis is anchored in examples that make explicit the social materiality of this blocking, citing the “disaster of access to vaccines during Covid-19” as evidence of the patent latifundium<1><2>259</2></1> <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 36)</4>. Mention is also made of the attempt to patent the “one-click” mechanism as a deliberate gesture to prevent the diffusion of a basic organizational improvement <5>Dowbor</5><6>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 22-23)</6>. Such cases function as concrete demonstrations of a <7>p. 240</7> single operative principle: when IP is mobilized to prevent the generalization of a technique, it ceases to reward creation and comes to administer deliberate scarcity in contexts in which diffusion would be socially desirable. The argumentative axis maintains, therefore, that the distinctive mark of rentier IP is not the recognition of the invention, but the strategic blocking of the learning and collective fertilization that the invention could generate.

The effect of rentier IP is not exhausted in the binary turnstile of “having” or “not having” access. When exclusivity multiplies and overlaps in layers, it ceases to function only as a gate and comes to operate as an engineering of friction. It distributes veto powers, makes recombinations more expensive and transforms incremental innovation into permanent negotiation. The consequence is competitive, by creating barriers to entry and favoring incumbents, and also distributive, by reproducing the technological gap as dependence.

The notion of authorization points becomes particularly visible in IOCs because enjoyment is not sustained as a unit exhaustible upon delivery, but as insertion in a governed process. In this process, availability, compatibility and continuity depend on external controls under the supplier's dominion <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 40; p. 51-52)</2>. Within the scope adopted here, this process manifests itself through the overlapping of layers of control bearing on the same experience. One may cite, for example, <3>software</3> and code, content protected by copyright, distinctive signs, <4>design</4> and contractual license regimes, so that each layer can operate as a basis for restricting, modulating or charging for uses and circulations.

The architecture of cumulative permissions comes close to the diagnosis that tangles of legal restrictions and transaction costs can produce underuse and blockages through an excess of vetoes, to the detriment of recombination and subsequent innovation <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 44; p. 47)</2>, and helps to explain why economic activity comes to depend on persistent legal mediations even in trivial operations of production and circulation <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 45-46)</4>. For consumption, the relevant effect is that the sign of “product” can conceal an enjoyment governed by partial authorizations, reinforcing the need to make verifiable, in terms of auditability, the restrictions actually bearing on the promised utility when governance by titles, licenses and access controls degrades the functional value of the experience.

The theoretical consequence is an inversion. What appears as a product in commercial discourse, in practice, comes to function as a bundle of fragmented, revocable and conditional authorizations. When the experience depends on successive keys (accounts, licenses, DRMs, authentications, terms, sanctions etc.), the market ceases to revolve around property and <1>p. 241</1> circulation and comes to revolve around governance and control. Thus, competition is no longer only a contest over supply, it becomes a contest over who can impose the most effective package of dependencies without losing social legitimacy.

It is precisely at this point that the discussion ceases to be whether we are “against or in favor of intellectual property” and becomes “how can we calibrate intellectual property teleologically”. Because, if the real economic function of enclosure is to reinstall scarcity where technique would dissolve price, the relevant legal problem becomes measuring up to what point exclusivity is still an incentive, and from what moment it becomes a structural toll. The question is not moral; it is one of institutional design, especially when the platform already dominates access and manages to convert any legal friction into competitive advantage.

Dowbor's propositional axis emerges when he gathers explicit alternatives for confronting this regime. Socializing innovation and preserving access does not depend on denying the remuneration of creative labor, but on disarticulating the normative equivalence between payment and blocking. For this reason, he reaffirms public access to knowledge as a structuring vector, by maintaining that knowledge generated with public resources must be socially accessible and serve the common good, and that access to knowledge and connectivity today constitutes a fundamental human right <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 62)</2>. In the same vein, he asserts that copyright must be limited, since the objective of copyright is to ensure reasonable remuneration for the author, and not to guarantee permanent rent for the intermediary, which is why he proposes a temporal limitation, even on the order of five years <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 43)</4>.

Exclusivity, in this framework, is not justified as prolonged retention, but as a functional and temporary measure. Intermediaries and chains of exploitation remain remunerable, but capture must occur through mechanisms compatible with circulation and access, and not through permanent tolls <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 64)</2>. The legal meaning of the inflection is to break the naturalization of enclosure as an ordinary technique of monetization. It is a matter of remunerating without hindering<3><4>260</4></3> and financing without blocking, rebuilding the balance between incentive and circulation in a regime marked by the non-rivalry of knowledge.

<1>p. 242</1> Dowbor does not offer a simplistic critique of intellectual property. On the contrary, he recognizes the historical legitimacy of the incentive, understood as privileged remuneration of the inventor or author, so as to stimulate scientific and cultural advances<2><3>261</3></2> <4>Dowbor</4><5>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 36)</5>. The turning point, however, occurs when the instrument loses social validity by turning into rentier charging for access. In this key, patents and <6>copyrights</6> cease to operate predominantly as a temporary technique of stimulus and come to function as a mechanism of blocking and toll on knowledge, including when effective ownership shifts to intermediaries and economic groups <7>Dowbor</7><8>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 36; p. 43; p. 46)</8>.

The critique, therefore, does not deny IP, but brings its legitimacy back to its purposive foundation. Intellectual property rights are not based on a natural right of property, but on their potential to stimulate future creativity <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 46)</2>. It follows that the hypertrophy of duration and scope produces teleological maladjustment and requires proportionality control when exclusivity becomes autonomous from the incentive and comes to operate as a fence <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 43)</4>. Within the present scope, this brings back the need to define criteria of loyalty, material transparency and preservation of the functional minimum legitimately expected in consumption environments mediated by platforms.

At this point, it becomes evident that the competitive mutation of immaterial markets does not stem from a “natural evolution” of the market, but from the convergence between technical infrastructure and legal infrastructure. The platform concentrates the mediation of access, the contract disciplines everyday use, and intellectual property provides the grammar of blocking that transforms circulation into exception and authorization into rule. The result is a regime in which market power is measured less by the capacity to produce goods and more by the capacity to <1>p. 243</1> administer gates, conditionalities and revocations, that is, to govern consumption as a permanently controllable process.

Having established the competitive mutation and the role of intellectual property as a component of enclosure coupled with infrastructure, it becomes possible to understand the reasons why, in continuous immaterial objects, the stability of value and the contestability of changes cease to be market noise and become part of the core of the legal problem under discussion.
