The metaphor of the “legal latifundium”, in Dowbor, describes a teleological dysfunction internal to the Intellectual Property regime: situations in which exclusivity, through hypertrophy of scope, duration and chains of licenses, ceases to operate predominantly as a temporary technique for stimulating future creativity and comes to function as a mechanism of artificial retention of social utility and of charging tolls on access, recombination and diffusion of technically reproducible knowledge <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 44-45)</2>. For this reason, the critique does not deny IP as a legal technique, but brings its legitimacy back to the purposive foundation that the author makes explicit: “The intellectual property right is not based on the natural right of property, but on its potential to stimulate future creativity.” <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 46)</4>. The dysfunction worsens when appropriation shifts systematically from the creator to intermediaries, composing the figure of the “absentee owner”: “Copyrights are largely assumed by those who hold the copyright or the patents, and in this case they are almost always intermediaries.” <5>Dowbor</5><6>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 43)</6>. In this scenario, the title of exclusivity tends to operate as an economic and institutional bottleneck in the final product, conditioning subsequent trajectories of innovation and access to the private control of permissions and licenses, with potential for disproportionate enrichment by position in the circuit <7>Dowbor</7><8>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 48-49; p. 58)</8>. <9>↩</9>

The metaphor of the “fence” can be read in a historical-institutional key as a reference to the lexicon of <1>enclosure</1>. Processes of legal privatization of common uses through titling and exclusion, not to transplant agrarian history to the digital, but to illuminate a recurrent structure of producing rent through the restriction of access. In Dowbor, “fence” designates the teleological inflection in which copyright ceases to operate predominantly as an incentive and comes to function as a perimeter barring access <2>Dowbor</2><3>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 44)</3>, articulating with the general mechanism of converting the reproducibility of the immaterial into monetizable artificial scarcity, that is, transforming technical abundance into rarefaction by institutional decision <4>Dowbor</4><5>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 23)</5>. <6>↩</6>

The notion of the “legal materiality” of the IOC, in Dowbor, can be understood as the institutional concreteness of enjoyment. The utility of the immaterial object depends on the governed continuity of access and on the stability of the technical-organizational rules that structure availability, compatibility and modification, and not on the digital medium itself <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51-52)</2>. The structural point is that this stability is anchored in infrastructures under private control, so that the “productive infrastructure […] is controlled by platforms, computers, algorithms and artificial intelligence”. <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 8)</4>. For this reason, the instability of these rules reconfigures, in practice, the functional value delivered to the consumer and makes enjoyment dependent on continuous governance in process <5>Dowbor</5><6>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51-52)</6>. <7>↩</7>

“Symbolic surplus”, within this scope, designates the value produced in the very use and circulation of signs within the ecosystem (reputation, belonging, styles, narratives and visibility), which is coupled to the IOC as its semiotic core and densifies enjoyment, raising its economic utility through retention, engagement and monetization. Dowbor situates the corresponding shift in following Gorz, by recording that “Gorz naturally moves on to analyze the function of the brand, of advertising, of symbolic values as the basis of the new formation of value” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 23)</2> and that, in the contemporary mutation, “The theory of value, the basis of economic science, shifts” <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 23)</4>, toward a regime in which exchange value is anchored “mainly, by its content of knowledge, information, general intelligence” <5>Dowbor</5><6>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 23)</6>. In this key, the institutional problem is not the existence of symbolic circulation in itself, but the possibility of its capture by contractual and IP fences and by asymmetric governance of visibility and access, reconverting diffuse contribution into an exclusive asset and recurrent rent; the logic of the “bottleneck” and the “toll” that falls on socially cumulative accumulations provides the structural model of this appropriation <7>Dowbor</7><8>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 48-49)</8>. In IOC ecosystems, the practical consequence is that the symbolic surplus formed in enjoyment can assume patrimonial and identity density for the consumer, while remaining vulnerable to private decisions of moderation, discontinuation or blocking, reinforcing the need for control of abusiveness and of material transparency when participation is organized as an engine of valorization of the ecosystem, but unilaterally appropriated by institutional design. <9>↩</9>

In contractual terms, the presence of clauses on user-generated content (UGC) is not, in itself, unlawful, since it may fulfill operational functions of hosting, making available and circulating content in digital ecosystems. The relevant legal problem arises when the design of the license exceeds this purpose and converts cultural participation into an asset appropriable in an asymmetric way, through broad and scarcely reciprocal authorizations, under unilateral governance of continuity, visibility and economic exploitation. In that case, the user's contribution ceases to operate as a community element densifying enjoyment and comes to be requalified as a proprietary input, articulating with Dowbor's diagnosis of the reorganization of value formation around brand, advertising and symbolic values <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 23)</2> and of the dependence, in the immaterial, on institutional mechanisms blocking diffusion in order to stabilize monetization <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 41)</4>. <5>↩</5>

Dowbor's critique of intellectual property rights bears on teleological dysfunctions internal to the very legal regime of its institutes. If exclusivity is legitimized by its instrumental function of stimulating future creativity, the extension of control beyond the typical period of recovery of investment tends to reduce the marginal gain of incentive and to operate as continued rent by position <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 46)</2>. In the case of copyright, the author observes that the realization of profits is concentrated in the first cycles of exploitation, while legal exclusivity may last for decades, converting the remaining protection into a barrier to access, with relevant social costs for cultural diffusion, recombination and licensing, without proportional benefit in new creations <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 43)</4>. This asymmetry reinforces the need to read the social function of IP, in platform environments, as a criterion for containing enclosures that come to operate as a toll on technically facilitated circulation, shifting the discussion from the isolated “title” to the institutional architecture that produces blocking, opacity and capture of value in the intangible <5>Dowbor</5><6>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 43; p. 46)</6>. <7>↩</7>

The concept of the tragedy of the anticommons, formulated by Michael Heller and developed with Rebecca Eisenberg, describes a regime in which the fragmentation of exclusivity rights distributes among multiple holders veto powers over parts, layers or components of the same resource, so that efficient use depends less on technical feasibility and more on costly legal coordination; the typical consequence is underuse through an excess of vetoes, because the sum of authorizations, licenses and negotiations becomes improbable or economically prohibitive. Dowbor mobilizes Boyle's synthesis to record this effect as a “tragedy of the anticommons”, associating it with the transaction costs generated by a “myriad” of property rights and with the result of restricting innovation by placing multiple obstacles in the path of subsequent developments <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 47)</2>, a diagnosis reinforced by the idea that the “tangle of legal restrictions” can reach a point at which it “hinders more than it stimulates research” <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 44)</4>. In contrast with the “tragedy of the commons” (exhaustion through excessive use when governance is lacking), the anticommons points to paralysis through hypertrophied governance, in the form of exclusivities and licenses that come to operate predominantly as a systemic locking of research, access and recombination. <5>↩</5>

The “patent latifundium” makes it possible to show, by way of example, the loss of proportionality between exclusivity and the corresponding social benefit when barriers persist even under collective urgency: in Dowbor's diagnosis, the “disaster of access to vaccines during Covid-19” exposes how patents can “immobilize” essential technology and organize a “war to hinder access” as a mechanism of rent, including under pressure from shareholders for dividends to the detriment of access pacts <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 36; p. 54)</2>. The usefulness of the example lies in showing that exclusivity can become autonomous from its justification and operate as a social and economic toll on diffusion, access and public response capacity, reinstating the social function of IP as a criterion of limitation and institutional calibration <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 46)</4>. <5>↩</5>

It should be noted that the legal system itself already contains calibration valves between incentive and circulation, allowing creation and innovation to be remunerated without depending on the blocking of access. Dowbor, on the one hand, observes that “openness in itself has become a powerful (and impressively beneficial) incentive” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 38)</2> and, on the other, maintains that remuneration can be organized at another point in the economic chain, preventing long and hypertrophied exclusivities from becoming a permanent toll <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 64)</4>. Within this horizon, various legally accommodable institutional arrangements appear, including funding policies and public procurement, in which remuneration occurs through distributive and public policy mechanisms, consistently with the role of collectively funded basic science and with the circulation of the result as a common good without prejudice to the payment of creative labor <5>Dowbor</5><6>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 6; p. 39)</6>; remunerated compulsory licenses and sectoral flexibilities as an exceptional technique to overcome bottlenecks and enable technology transfer in the face of global challenges, including solutions such as pools and access-oriented flexibilities <7>Dowbor</7><8>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 53)</8>; and open licensing models and collective forms of management, which reduce transaction costs and avoid systemic blockages by shifting remuneration to services, curation, maintenance and complementary activities <9>Dowbor</9><10>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 43-44; p. 64)</10>. Together, the instruments show that IP, read through its social function, admits degrees of exclusivity and instruments of teleological correction when hypertrophied exclusivity comes to operate as a structural barrier to cultural circulation, recombination and public access <11>Dowbor</11><12>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 43-44; p. 64)</12>. <13>↩</13>

Dowbor recognizes the historical justification of intellectual protection as a technique of incentive — privileged remuneration of the inventor and the author to stimulate scientific and cultural advances —, but maintains that, in the contemporary configuration, patents and copyrights tend to operate as a rentier mechanism of charging for access and blocking the diffusion of knowledge <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 36)</2>. The author exemplifies the dysfunction by the temporal inadequacy of the patent in the face of the technological pace, pointing to the experience of the Covid-19 pandemic as a case of socially disastrous restriction of access, and by the expansion of copyright with economic concentration in publishers, not in authors, illustrating with the horizon of open access to the works of Paulo Freire only in 2067 <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 36)</4>. In this diagnosis, the “war to hinder access” becomes a central axis of the knowledge economy, while mechanisms of openness (Open Access, Creative Commons and the like) figure as an institutional alternative capable of radically expanding worldwide access to knowledge without depending on retention as the ordinary form of remuneration <5>Dowbor</5><6>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 36)</6>. <7>↩</7>

<1>Abusive teleology</1>

The image of the contemporary fief becomes more than a metaphor when one observes the real structure of the bond in platform-operated games. The territory is not an “open market”, but a space enclosed by account, access structure, terms of use, curation of access and its own mechanisms of sanction, so that the consumer's permanence depends on continuous authorization and on conformity to a practical normativity. Tribute presents itself as fulfillment of a requirement in attention and dedication, microtransaction, pass, subscription or purchase of signs of distinction, while the decree manifests itself as <1>patch</1>, <2>rework</2> and unilateral reconfiguration of internal economies that alter the substance of enjoyment without formally extinguishing the nominal ownership of the good. The feudal logic, in this sense, does not describe a medievalizing aesthetic, but a form of economic organization in which the platform holds the monopoly of infrastructure and the power to rewrite, over time, the material conditions of valorization and of the existence of consumption.

Digital platforms can be understood as teleological architectures of continuous extraction, institutional and technical-functional designs aimed at stabilizing rent and power in markets for immaterial goods, shifting economic command from the product to the conditions of access, permanence and circulation. The dialectical reading of Varoufakis <1>(2024)</1> and Dowbor <2>(2024)</2>, combined with the structural homology of the lumpenproletariat in Marx <3>(2011; 2013)</3>, makes it possible to reconstruct, in layers, the economic core that sustains this form of power.

For Varoufakis, the key is the shift of command to infrastructure. The platform ceases to be merely a company that sells a product and comes to operate as an informational landlord that controls the conditions of entry, permanence and circulation in a governed environment. The figure of the “cloud serf” does not function here as a moral metaphor, but as a social form derived from a market in which enjoyment depends on continuous private intermediation and in which exit becomes costly through loss of history, repertoire, reputation, <1>p. 244</1> ties and accumulated investments, including in the form of identity and symbolic capital objectified in progress, collections, public performance records and signs of status in the ecosystem.

Dowbor offers the meso-structural register of this transformation by describing informational rentierism as a mode of extraction based on “turnstiles” and “tolls”, in which rent shifts from the act of producing to the act of controlling passage. The platform stabilizes value not through natural rarity of the object, but through institutionally produced rarefaction, coupled with authorization regimes and legal-technical mechanisms that reintroduce friction where technique would tend toward abundance. In this framework, monetization ceases to be a simple price and assumes the form of recurrent charging for permanence, for continuity and for predictability of access, that is, for governed enjoyment itself.

This institutionally produced rarefaction is not sustained only by commercial decisions or by “market” scarcity, but by a legal-technical enclosure of the informational. Intellectual property mechanisms, articulated with contractual licensing regimes, technological restriction measures and interoperability controls, operate as an institutional technology of governance of circulation, since they transform reproduction into authorization, use into revocable permission and access into a continually renegotiable condition. By reintroducing friction where technique would tend toward abundance, this enclosure stabilizes the capacity to impose tolls, modulate the experience and prevent alternative forms of enjoyment and competition, making control of access an asset as valuable as, or more valuable than, the immaterial object itself.

Marx, in turn, presents a critical instrument for identifying the point at which consumption ceases to be mere expenditure and comes to function as invisible production. The platform does not extract value only when it receives payment, but when it captures activity, including the time, attention, conduct, symbolic validation and social participation of users, then converted into data, metrics, network effects and competitive advantages. The user appears formally as external to the wage relationship, but is materially incorporated into the regime of valorization as an unrecognized productive exterior, providing the continuous input that feeds the machine of monetization and governance.

From this convergence, the business model of platforms can be described as an architecture of continuous extraction applied to ontologically non-scarce goods. Its stability depends on three structural operators that act in an integrated way: production of artificial scarcity, manufacture of risk as a discipline of presence and capture of the user's diffuse productivity as economic and semiotic input. The platform does not <1>p. 245</1> limit itself to offering goods and services. It governs the conditions of enjoyment, converting access into permanence and circulation into authorization.

The articulation between artificial scarcity, manufactured risk and diffuse productivity makes it possible to understand why, in IOC markets, competition tends to take on the character of a tournament and concentration becomes structural. When the platform holds the infrastructure of circulation and the grammar of symbolic value (by defining what counts as rarity, what counts as <1>status</1>, what counts as <2>meta</2> and what counts as belonging), it transforms competition into a contest over ecosystems and over governance capacity, and not over isolated products. Whoever wins the contest over the ecosystem comes to hold not only market share, but the power to impose conditions of access, permanence and visibility, reorganizing behaviors at scale and converting private rules into competitive advantage.

This feeds back into a captivity of demand: switching costs, functional and symbolic dependencies, network externalities and accumulated investments make exit costly and permanence structurally probable. In this scenario, artificial scarcity is not a <1>marketing</1> expedient. It is the instrument for stabilizing power.

This stabilization is not explained only by “consumer preferences” or by superior efficiency in an isolated product. It is explained by the fact that, in the immaterial realm, control of the environment can coincide with control of the market itself. The route of access to the object is, at the same time, the private infrastructure that organizes its enjoyment and administers the conditions of circulation. Competition then shifts to the contest over command of gates, protocols, interfaces, catalogs, recommendation regimes and rules of permanence, that is, over control of devices that function as essential market infrastructure. Economic power comes to reside in the capacity to define the possible experience, modulate the time of enjoyment, impose exit costs and produce functional and symbolic dependencies that, in practice, convert formal freedom of choice into governed permanence.

Artificial scarcity is the first operator of this architecture because it reinserts rarity where technology would tend toward abundance. In immaterial goods, reproducibility puts pressure on price and dissolves natural rarity, so that it becomes functional to produce rarefaction by institutional decision, by means of windows and rotations of availability, temporary exclusivities, seasons and limited events, access tiers, countdowns, editions and forms of conditional acquisition. Scarcity, here, does not describe the object, since it describes the access regime and is a mode of governing circulation.

Manufactured risk is the second operator, since it converts the access regime into a practical discipline of return and presence. The relevant risk is not only the classic risk of the product's <1>p. 246</1> malfunctioning, but the risk of missing an opportunity, of falling behind and of suffering symbolic and functional depreciation within the ecosystem, with the evaporation of value accumulated in the form of status, repertoire, progress and belonging. This grammar of risk is produced by recurrent mechanisms, such as imposed schedules, with seasons, availability windows, rotations and limited events, sanctions and downgrades, with loss of position, visibility, rewards or access to certain layers of the service, and planned uncertainty, with opaque criteria, unilateral modulation of rules and calculated instability of what counts as <2>meta</2> or as value. By organizing the experience as continuous administration of the possibility of loss, the platform creates an environment in which permanence ceases to be an episodic option and comes to operate as rational conduct protecting investments and position, so that consumption ceases to be an event and comes to function as a routine.

Diffuse productivity is the third operator, since it closes the economic circuit without depending exclusively on payment. The user's activity sustains the ecosystem and is converted into an asset, into data and metrics, social proof and diffusion, symbolic validation, network effects, patterns of comparison and hierarchies of visibility. In this arrangement, the user is not merely a recipient of an offer, because he participates materially in the valorization of the environment that governs him. This participation need not appear as labor to operate as input, since it manifests itself as capturable and recombinable presence, circulation and conduct, feeding monetization strategies and the very competitive stabilization of the platform.

The question is thus objectively detached from the moral dimension and becomes a legal-structural one. The diagnosis does not depend on attributing the phenomenon to “compulsive consumption” or to “bad choices”, because the relevant coercion does not present itself as an explicit imposition of purchase, but as dependence produced by design, by governance and by narratives that organize value and belonging within a closed circuit.

The economic architecture of the platform contains a teleology of continuous extraction that materializes in recurrent mechanisms. Among them is the unilateral modulation of the conditions of enjoyment, with alteration of rules, prices, access tiers, ranking criteria and recommendation regimes. Also present are functional opacities that prevent verification and contestation, such as non-auditable criteria, informational asymmetries and uncertainty about what determines results. Added to this, finally, is the continuous calibration of behavior, by means of A/B tests, gamification and selective frictions that make certain paths natural and others costly. When the consumer is kept as a serf of the infrastructure by means of artificial scarcity and manufactured risk, the legal question ceases to be <1>p. 247</1> merely contractual and becomes one of the legitimacy of the architecture, that is, of the economic purpose incorporated into the normal mode of functioning of the service.

This structure explains why, in the illustrative scenario of the thesis, the player's frustration is not mere subjective “displeasure”, but a symptom of an economy of power in which the consumer does not merely buy an item, but enters and invests in a governed regime of belonging that has a direct interest in modulating his emotions through cycles of satisfaction and frustration. The <1>rework</1> that redesigns a character, effects and position in the metagame is functionally equivalent to a reordering of the territory that devalues past investments without offering an internal mechanism of value equivalence, and without allowing the consumer to take what he acquired outside the platform's jurisdiction. The contemporary fief is sustained precisely by this asymmetry, since exit is formally possible, but economically irrational when reputation, history, ties, signs of distinction and acquired goods remain trapped in the same technical enclosure.

The closer the platform comes to practical sovereignty over access, visibility and the meaning of what was acquired, the more the axis of protection needs to bear on integrity, restoration and controllability, and not on a narrow notion of one-off delivery.

The question that arises, therefore, is to what extent Law can impose limits on business models that, in order to monetize the immaterial, need to transform access into dependence, promise into a permanent cycle and enjoyment into a toll circuit. The problem shifts from the atomized examination of events and clauses to the evaluation of the economic purpose incorporated into the arrangement, that is, to the examination of an institutional design that produces continuous extraction as a normal result of its functioning. This purpose is not sustained only by direct economic coercions, but by the administration of the social conditions of recognition of value within the ecosystem. The closing mechanism of this economic architecture is the governance of the visible, the desirable and the recognizable, by which technical abundance is converted into socially perceived scarcity and belonging is transformed into a discipline of permanence.

So far, the analysis has established that the platform does not act as a simple “contractual model” aimed at a one-off purchase, since it is a mode of production that organizes enjoyment as administered permanence. Thus, extraction is not concentrated in the act of sale, since it tends to stabilize as recurrent rent through access and <1>p. 248</1> tolls, supported by artificial scarcity, manufactured risk, competition by enclosure and architectural teleology, with intellectual property operating as a technology for blocking and closing off the field. In this arrangement, economic power does not derive only from clauses or prices, but from the continuous governance of the conditions of existence of the object and of the consumer bond itself, keeping the consumer bound to a territory in which utility, rarity and value can be reprogrammed by unilateral decision presented as technical routine.

If extraction under platforms depends on permanence and on governance of access, it needs to govern the field in which this permanence is decided in practice, that of attention and signification. The platform economy is sustained by regulating what gains salience and what becomes socially desirable, because it is on this plane that it is decided what appears as valuable, what seems inevitable, what deserves time and what yields belonging. The key is neither price nor initial delivery, but the capacity to organize the horizon of what counts as object, as choice and as value.

In the classical market, economic discipline operates above all through price variation and competitive pressure, the axis on which access, substitution and preference are resolved. On platforms, discipline is reconfigured, since everyday experience is mediated by discovery devices and visibility metrics that not only organize the offer, but construct the field of what seems to exist and to matter. Power is not limited to charging or prohibiting, since it is exercised by defining what is seen, what is comparable, what is desirable and what gains social traction, pushing certain alternatives toward “naturalness” and others toward practical invisibility. Economy and semiotics cease to be parallel layers, because regulating perception, comparison and visibility is regulating the decision field itself.

The utility of a good is not reduced to physical use, because of its function as an infrastructure of classification and communication<1><2>262</2></1>. Goods stabilize hierarchies, boundaries of <3>p. 249</3> belonging and the intelligibility of the social world by providing marking services capable of organizing calendars, estimating relations and sustaining reciprocities <4>Isherwood</4><5>(Douglas; Isherwood, 1996, p. xxii; p. 40-41)</5>. From this perspective, the relevance lies in offering a vocabulary for describing the immaterial object of consumption as something whose social utility depends on social legibility and belonging within an administered ecosystem, which allows the exit cost to be read not only as patrimonial loss, but as a risk of isolation and weakened bonds.

The central consequence of this approach is that meaning does not reside in an isolated item, but in the relational grammar of the whole. Goods operate as the <1>hardware</1> and <2>software</2> of an informational system in which meaning emerges from the relations<3><4>263</4></3> between things, and not from an essence stuck to each object <5>Isherwood</5><6>(Douglas; Isherwood, 1996, p. 49)</6>. In platform environments, this gives the problem operational precision. Regulating curation and windows of circulation is equivalent to regulating the grammar by which value and belonging are expressed, because it alters the relations that make the collection “say” something. When the good is inseparable from its visibility, comparability and recognition, the ecosystem that administers the conditions of appearance comes to administer the sign together with enjoyment. What is delivered is not just an item. The conditions of language that make this item exist as a socially legible difference within this ecosystem are maintained, or reordered.

Along the same line, “attention economy” ceases to be a metaphor. The decisive scarce resource is not the technical availability of the good, but the user's exposure time. Retention provides volume for observation, profiling, continuous testing of stimuli and calibration of triggers. It is this predictability that stabilizes extraction through subscription, pass, “unmissable event”, rotation of offer and successive tolls. Without captured and <1>p. 250</1> governed attention, recurrent rent loses support, because access ceases to operate as a maintenance fee for one's place and tends to return to the appearance of an episodic purchase.

This transition calls for a language<1><2>264</2></1> capable of treating value as a result of situated recognition, and not as an intrinsic attribute. In this key, circulation creates value and the link between exchange and value is political in a broad sense. The consequence is that the relevant question ceases to be “how much does it cost” and becomes “which frames make something appear as desirable, comparable and rare”, because value is not inherent in the object, but a judgment<3><4>265</4></3> produced by subjects and endorsed by a real or imagined exchange <5>Appadurai</5><6>(Appadurai, 1986, p. 3-4)</6>. For this reason, the author prefers to speak of regimes of value, whose coherence<7><8>266</8></7> may vary according to the situation and according to the commodity, without requiring full cultural consensus to operate <9>Appadurai</9><10>(Appadurai, 1986, p. 14-15)</10>.

<1>p. 251</1> The notion of “politics of value”<2><3>267</3></2> makes explicit the field of power that sustains these regimes. Ordinary exchange depends on agreements about what is desirable and also about who can exercise effective demand and under what circumstances <4>Appadurai</4><5>(Appadurai, 1986, p. 57)</5>. On platforms, this link thickens, because <6>gatekeeping</6> does not bear only on price or contract. It bears on the conditions of visibility that make a sign desirable and a good demandable, converting control of circulation into control of value. If value is an effect of situated recognition, administering catalog, rarity and rules of visibility (curation, windows, criteria) is administering the practical conditions of value itself.

This point becomes even more incisive when consumption is treated as a mechanism of belonging. Douglas and Isherwood <1>(1996, p. xxiv)</1> describe goods as devices of alignment and boundary. Social life is organized by signs of adherence and exclusion, and goods function as public marks that raise fences against the unwanted, consolidating solidarities and demarcating “<2>keep out” signs</2>. In this framework, the correct measure of poverty is not possession, but social involvement, because participation in the informational circuit of consumption determines access to support, predictability and capacity to act <3>Isherwood</3><4>(Douglas; Isherwood, 1996, p. xiv; p. xxii)</4>. Being out of reach of this system is not a subjective discomfort. It is a risk of practical silencing<5><6>268</6></5>, reduction of voice and of future options, with direct impact on the very rationality of choice <7>Isherwood</7><8>(Douglas; Isherwood, 1996, p. 63-65)</8>.

<1>p. 252</1> From this follows a functional thesis for the immaterial object of consumption. When the good depends on appearing, being recognized and circulating in order to “be worth” something, the governance of belonging is converted into a technique of permanence. Rentierism in the immaterial is only sustained when technical abundance is translated into social scarcity. The platform installs a regime of comparison of rarity, status and opportunity, which makes access seem a condition of the existence of value, and not a whim of the <2>gatekeeper</2>. Without this regime, charging for access appears as irritation and permanence loses meaning. With it, the toll becomes a maintenance fee for one's place, because what is lost on leaving is not only functional utility, but the very social intelligibility of the collection and of the signs it emits.

In terms of the structure of the object, this reconnects the category of the Immaterial Object of Consumption to its semiotic condition of existence. The IOC does not behave as a “good” only through an isolated functional utility, but as a functional and semiotic bundle, in which enjoyment depends on operations of public legibility and collective recognition. Thus, governing signs, regimes of appearance and collective recognition is not a gesture external to supply, but a way of governing the object itself and its utility over time, because it is in this field that what “counts” as relevant difference, socially perceived rarity and belonging is formed.

The discussion gains an additional tool for describing mutations of value over time without resorting to morality or psychology. In this sense, the perspective of the culturally informed economic <3>p. 253</3> biography<1><2>269</2></1> treats<4><5>270</5></4> the object as a culturally constructed entity, endowed with specific meanings and classified and reclassified into socially constituted categories <6>Kopytoff</6><7>(Kopytoff, 1986, p. 68)</7>. The fact that an object is bought or exchanged says nothing about its later status, since it can be withdrawn from the sphere of exchange and still retain commodity potential and latent exchange value<8><9>271</9></8> <10>Kopytoff</10><11>(Kopytoff, 1986, p. 75-76)</11>.

For the immaterial object of consumption, this describes precisely why <1>reworks</1>, relaunches, trivializations and repositionings alter value and status without the item “disappearing”. The platform operates as a practical institution of singularization, asserting power through the competence to reclassify, that is, to insist on the right to singularize<2><3>272</3></2> a class of objects and to control public institutions<4><5>273</5></4> of singularization (Kopytoff, 1986, p. <6>p. 254</6> 73; p. 81). On platforms, this singularization takes the form of catalog retirement, changes in rarity, restrictions on obtaining items, event-based repositioning, recoding by <7>meta</7> and rearrangement of display criteria. The user's nominal ownership is maintained, but the cultural biography of the item is materially reordered, and it is this biography that sustains social utility, prestige and equivalence between promise and delivery.

When the efficient risk is losing <1>timing</1>, <2>status</2> and belonging, the discipline of presence installs itself as a technique of governing time. Absence ceases to be a mere interruption and comes to produce measurable decline, progressive erasure and practical discontinuity, making permanence the rational way of avoiding loss. The risk is semiotic and temporal by structure. It is semiotic because it depends on the social meaning of what is lost, and temporal because it functions through windows, calendars, cycles and rhythms that convert delay into objective disadvantage even when the immaterial object remains technically accessible.

At this point, consumption reveals itself as ritual<1><2>274</2></1> in a technical sense, a mechanism that fixes public meanings and stabilizes classifications. Douglas and Isherwood <3>(1996, p. 43)</3> formulate this by treating goods as ritual adjuncts and consumption as a ritual process whose function is to produce meaning in the unstable flow of events, containing the drift of meanings through visible public conventions. Consumption makes judgments firm and visible in the continuous classification of persons and events, which allows demand to be understood as a social, relational and active phenomenon, and not as a private and atomic act (Douglas; Isherwood, <4>p. 255</4> 1996, p. 45; p. viii-ix). This definition also connects rite and bond operationally by treating goods as providers of marking services in consumption rituals, capable of drawing a cartography of social integration through the standardized flow of goods <5>Isherwood</5><6>(Douglas; Isherwood, 1996, p. xxii)</6>.

In platform ecosystems, routines such as daily login, missions, limited-time events, seasons and passes can be read as operationalized ritualization. Attendance is organized as a condition of participation in a public system of marking in which value, reputation and belonging are continually confirmed. The typical punishment need not present itself as a direct sanction, because the administered rite already produces the effect of loss of position and loss of voice. Absence is equivalent to being outside the informational system that allows one to hear and be heard, with harm to the very capacity of choice <1>Isherwood</1><2>(Douglas; Isherwood, 1996, p. 63-65)</2>.

Symbolic charging emerges when consumption operates as a social obligation coupled to the bond. It is a system of reciprocal rituals that implies expenditures to mark occasions, guests and hosts, or the community in general. When consumption is the “normal” mark of friendship, falling out of step with the rhythm of the circuit produces weakened access to information and support, surprise in the face of crises and less readiness to deal with the situation <1>Isherwood</1><2>(Douglas; Isherwood, 1996, p. xxii)</2>.

On platforms, the question paves the way for the discussion of the identity cost of exit. Permanence is not sustained only by money already spent, but because withdrawal implies discontinuity of biography and loss of social legibility. Repertoire, history, network, collection and public signs accumulated as proof of trajectory and belonging are lost. The platform transforms invested time into a backing of socially objectified identity by organizing these elements as verifiable symbolic capital.
